newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission proposes joint approach to refugees' care.
newsitem.headline: Commission proposes joint approach to refugees' care.

text.p: People given temporary protection in a European Union country after fleeing problems back home should be given the right to work, send their children to school and have babies, the European Commission said on Wednesday.

Spurred on by the lack of a coordinated EU response when 800,000 people fled Bosnia to seek protection in the bloc, the Commission said the EU should adopt a joint action on temporary protection, guaranteeing basic rights.
"I do not think that what happened in Bosnia is going to be the last phenomenon of that kind," Justice Commissioner Anita Gradin told a news conference.

The proposal is not likely to affect any outflow of people from the Balkan state of Albania, mired in violent unrest, as it must be approved by the justice and home affairs council ministers and it will not be discussed by them until the end of May, Gradin said.

The Commission intends the proposal to complement rather than replace the 1951 Geneva convention on the status of refugees under which asylum seekers must be examined on a case by case basis by the host country.

When the number of asylum seekers is so great in a crisis that this kind of individual vetting is not realistic, and member states resort to temporary protection measures and at present each has different approaches.
In Denmark and Greece for example, people given temporary shelter have no possibility to work, while they can work in Sweden. In Finland they are entitled to unemployment benefits.
In Denmark, Greece and Luxembourg there is no right for a person to reunite their family, while the right does exist in Belgium and Ireland.
In Italy they have no right to social assistance, while France and Portugal have no official arrangement for giving their children schooling.
Once agreed the EU would set up a joint decision-making mechanism for opening up, prolonging and phasing out a temporary protection regime.
Under the proposal, the first for an EU instrument in the asylum field, the EU executive would every year report on the situation in refugees' country of origin as well as in each EU member state.
The Commission said it wanted to set a minimum threshold for basic rights and benefits for the people under protection.
"They should be able to support themselves, be able to reunite their immediate family at least, send their children to school," Gradin said.
